sources.title: Potty Training Regression
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: Your first response when this happens should be to have them examined by their pediatrician to be sure the cause is not physical. ... Change in the child-care routine—for example, a new sitter, or starting a child-care or preschool program ... Ask them why this might be—because their potty is in a new bathroom in your new home now, because the toilet at the child-care center is scary, or because their new baby brother wears a diaper and has been getting so much attention lately? Listen to their response ... Arrange for a special time to spend alone with your child (without her new sibling), accompany them to the child-care center to talk with caregivers about how they can help your child keep up their bathroom habits, or surround their potty in the new home with familiar objects from the old home. Ask your child to think of ideas, too, on how to improve their situation. ... Support them with positive reinforcements, including hugs and praise, stickers on a chart, and an occasional pep talk as they struggle to regain their footing. ... If your child’s regression stretches on for a month or more, you may need to ask yourself whether they were ready to be fully day-trained in the first place. There’s no harm in suggesting that you set the potty aside for a while if it’s clear that this would be a big relief to your child. ... Upsetting as regression can be to parents, it usually doesn’t last very long. In many cases, the child picks up where she left off in toilet training after a few days or weeks.
sources.supports: Check with the pediatrician first; a change like a new child-care routine or a new sibling is a common cause; ask the child why and listen; special time alone, familiar objects around the potty, talking with caregivers, asking the child for ideas; hugs, praise and stickers; a pause after a month or more; it usually does not last long. An American Academy of Pediatrics family page.

sources.title: Emotional Issues and Potty Training Problems
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: At about three years of age, children start developing the capacity to experience discomfort, or shame, when they have done something they know is wrong. ... They may hide their wet underwear, or even try to clean up the mess before you see it. There is no cause to criticize or punish a child who behaves in this way. ... The best response when you find your child hiding their accidents from you is to gently tell them that you know they had an accident, that it’s okay, and that you know they will do better next time. Then ask them to help you clean up, and talk with them about specific ways the two of you can help them get back on track. ... If they feel you have been too controlling about bathroom use—constantly asking if they need to go instead of letting them direct their own behavior—they may resist going until it’s too late and they have an accident instead. ... A more active imagination and a tendency toward magical thinking may cause them to fear the toilet and start to avoid it. ... Meanwhile, try to avoid major concessions such as returning to diapers. Instead, consider offering to put them in training pants under their underwear for a while, put the potty in their room, accompany them to the preschool bathroom before the school day begins, or otherwise compromise until they feel more secure.
sources.supports: From about age 3 children can feel shame after an accident and may hide it; do not criticize or punish; say you know, that it is okay and that next time will go better; ask for help cleaning up; constant asking can make a child hold back until it is too late; fear of the toilet; no return to diapers, training pants, the potty in the child's room, going with the child to the preschool bathroom. An American Academy of Pediatrics family page.

sources.title: Potty Training
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts, date reviewed March 2019)
sources.quote: Have your child sit on the potty within 15 to 30 minutes after meals to take advantage of the body's natural tendency to have a bowel movement after eating ... Avoid clothes that are hard to take off, such as overalls and shirts that snap in the crotch. Kids who are potty training need to be able to undress themselves. ... Offer your child small rewards, such as stickers or time reading, every time your child goes in the potty. Keep a chart to track of successes. Once your little one appears to be mastering the use of the toilet, let them pick out a few new pairs of big-kid underwear to wear. ... Make sure all caregivers — including babysitters, grandparents, and daycare workers — follow the same routine and use the same names for body parts and bathroom acts. ... Praise all attempts to use the toilet, even if nothing happens. And remember that accidents will happen. It's important not to punish potty-training children or show disappointment when they wet or soil themselves or the bed. Instead, tell your child that it was an accident and offer your support. sources.title: Emotional Issues and Potty Training Problems
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: At about three years of age, children start developing the capacity to experience discomfort, or shame, when they have done something they know is wrong. ... They may hide their wet underwear, or even try to clean up the mess before you see it. There is no cause to criticize or punish a child who behaves in this way. ... The best response when you find your child hiding their accidents from you is to gently tell them that you know they had an accident, that it’s okay, and that you know they will do better next time. Then ask them to help you clean up, and talk with them about specific ways the two of you can help them get back on track. ... If they feel you have been too controlling about bathroom use—constantly asking if they need to go instead of letting them direct their own behavior—they may resist going until it’s too late and they have an accident instead. ... A more active imagination and a tendency toward magical thinking may cause them to fear the toilet and start to avoid it. ... Meanwhile, try to avoid major concessions such as returning to diapers. Instead, consider offering to put them in training pants under their underwear for a while, put the potty in their room, accompany them to the preschool bathroom before the school day begins, or otherwise compromise until they feel more secure.
sources.supports: From about age 3 children can feel shame after an accident and may hide it; do not criticize or punish; say you know, that it is okay and that next time will go better; ask for help cleaning up; constant asking can make a child hold back until it is too late; fear of the toilet; no return to diapers, training pants, the potty in the child's room, going with the child to the preschool bathroom. An American Academy of Pediatrics family page.

sources.title: Potty Training
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts, date reviewed March 2019)
sources.quote: Have your child sit on the potty within 15 to 30 minutes after meals to take advantage of the body's natural tendency to have a bowel movement after eating ... Avoid clothes that are hard to take off, such as overalls and shirts that snap in the crotch. Kids who are potty training need to be able to undress themselves. ... Offer your child small rewards, such as stickers or time reading, every time your child goes in the potty. Keep a chart to track of successes. Once your little one appears to be mastering the use of the toilet, let them pick out a few new pairs of big-kid underwear to wear. ... Make sure all caregivers — including babysitters, grandparents, and daycare workers — follow the same routine and use the same names for body parts and bathroom acts. ... Praise all attempts to use the toilet, even if nothing happens. And remember that accidents will happen. It's important not to punish potty-training children or show disappointment when they wet or soil themselves or the bed. Instead, tell your child that it was an accident and offer your support. Reassure your child that he or she is well on the way to using the potty like a big kid. ... Many kids who've been using the potty have some trouble during times of stress. For example, a 2- or 3-year-old dealing with a new sibling may start having accidents.
sources.supports: Sit on the potty 15 to 30 minutes after meals, clothes that are easy to take off, small rewards like stickers or reading time and picking new underwear, the same routine for every caregiver, praise every attempt, no punishment and no disappointed face, say it was an accident and reassure the child, and that stress such as a new sibling can bring accidents back. A Nemours page for parents.

sources.title: Potty Training Regression
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: Your first response when this happens should be to have them examined by their pediatrician to be sure the cause is not physical. ... Change in the child-care routine—for example, a new sitter, or starting a child-care or preschool program ... Ask them why this might be—because their potty is in a new bathroom in your new home now, because the toilet at the child-care center is scary, or because their new baby brother wears a diaper and has been getting so much attention lately? Listen to their response ... Arrange for a special time to spend alone with your child (without her new sibling), accompany them to the child-care center to talk with caregivers about how they can help your child keep up their bathroom habits, or surround their potty in the new home with familiar objects from the old home. Ask your child to think of ideas, too, on how to improve their situation. ... Support them with positive reinforcements, including hugs and praise, stickers on a chart, and an occasional pep talk as they struggle to regain their footing. ... If your child’s regression stretches on for a month or more, you may need to ask yourself whether they were ready to be fully day-trained in the first place. There’s no harm in suggesting that you set the potty aside for a while if it’s clear that this would be a big relief to your child. ... Upsetting as regression can be to parents, it usually doesn’t last very long. In many cases, the child picks up where she left off in toilet training after a few days or weeks.
sources.supports: Check with the pediatrician first; a change like a new child-care routine or a new sibling is a common cause; ask the child why and listen; special time alone, familiar objects around the potty, talking with caregivers, asking the child for ideas; hugs, praise and stickers; a pause after a month or more; it usually does not last long. An American Academy of Pediatrics family page.

sources.title: Emotional Issues and Potty Training Problems
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: At about three years of age, children start developing the capacity to experience discomfort, or shame, when they have done something they know is wrong. ... They may hide their wet underwear, or even try to clean up the mess before you see it. There is no cause to criticize or punish a child who behaves in this way. ... The best response when you find your child hiding their accidents from you is to gently tell them that you know they had an accident, that it’s okay, and that you know they will do better next time. Then ask them to help you clean up, and talk with them about specific ways the two of you can help them get back on track. ... If they feel you have been too controlling about bathroom use—constantly asking if they need to go instead of letting them direct their own behavior—they may resist going until it’s too late and they have an accident instead. ... A more active imagination and a tendency toward magical thinking may cause them to fear the toilet and start to avoid it. ... Meanwhile, try to avoid major concessions such as returning to diapers. Instead, consider offering to put them in training pants under their underwear for a while, put the potty in their room, accompany them to the preschool bathroom before the school day begins, or otherwise compromise until they feel more secure.
sources.supports: From about age 3 children can feel shame after an accident and may hide it; do not criticize or punish; say you know, that it is okay and that next time will go better; ask for help cleaning up; constant asking can make a child hold back until it is too late; fear of the toilet; no return to diapers, training pants, the potty in the child's room, going with the child to the preschool bathroom. An American Academy of Pediatrics family page.

sources.title: Potty Training
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts, date reviewed March 2019)
sources.quote: Have your child sit on the potty within 15 to 30 minutes after meals to take advantage of the body's natural tendency to have a bowel movement after eating ... Avoid clothes that are hard to take off, such as overalls and shirts that snap in the crotch. Kids who are potty training need to be able to undress themselves. ... Offer your child small rewards, such as stickers or time reading, every time your child goes in the potty. Keep a chart to track of successes. Once your little one appears to be mastering the use of the toilet, let them pick out a few new pairs of big-kid underwear to wear. ... Make sure all caregivers — including babysitters, grandparents, and daycare workers — follow the same routine and use the same names for body parts and bathroom acts. ... Praise all attempts to use the toilet, even if nothing happens. And remember that accidents will happen. It's important not to punish potty-training children or show disappointment when they wet or soil themselves or the bed. Instead, tell your child that it was an accident and offer your support. Reassure your child that he or she is well on the way to using the potty like a big kid. ... Many kids who've been using the potty have some trouble during times of stress. For example, a 2- or 3-year-old dealing with a new sibling may start having accidents.
sources.supports: Sit on the potty 15 to 30 minutes after meals, clothes that are easy to take off, small rewards like stickers or reading time and picking new underwear, the same routine for every caregiver, praise every attempt, no punishment and no disappointed face, say it was an accident and reassure the child, and that stress such as a new sibling can bring accidents back. A Nemours page for parents.

sources.title: Potty Training Regression
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: Your first response when this happens should be to have them examined by their pediatrician to be sure the cause is not physical. ... Change in the child-care routine—for example, a new sitter, or starting a child-care or preschool program ... Ask them why this might be—because their potty is in a new bathroom in your new home now, because the toilet at the child-care center is scary, or because their new baby brother wears a diaper and has been getting so much attention lately? Listen to their response ... Arrange for a special time to spend alone with your child (without her new sibling), accompany them to the child-care center to talk with caregivers about how they can help your child keep up their bathroom habits, or surround their potty in the new home with familiar objects from the old home. Ask your child to think of ideas, too, on how to improve their situation. ... Support them with positive reinforcements, including hugs and praise, stickers on a chart, and an occasional pep talk as they struggle to regain their footing. ... If your child’s regression stretches on for a month or more, you may need to ask yourself whether they were ready to be fully day-trained in the first place. There’s no harm in suggesting that you set the potty aside for a while if it’s clear that this would be a big relief to your child. ... Upsetting as regression can be to parents, it usually doesn’t last very long. In many cases, the child picks up where she left off in toilet training after a few days or weeks.
sources.supports: Check with the pediatrician first; a change like a new child-care routine or a new sibling is a common cause; ask the child why and listen; special time alone, familiar objects around the potty, talking with caregivers, asking the child for ideas; hugs, praise and stickers; a pause after a month or more; it usually does not last long. An American Academy of Pediatrics family page.

sources.title: How to Help Kids Cope With Disappointment
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents, Katie Hurley, LCSW (16 Jan 2019)
sources.quote: With proper support and frequent discussions about coping with disappointment and overcoming obstacles, young children can learn how to handle life’s disappointments, big and small. ... Use empathic responses like, “I understand that this is difficult. I know you feel disappointed right now.” Give your child the time and space to cry, feel sad and soak up a hug from mom or dad. Connection helps kids recover from adversity. Meet heated responses with calm ones to model healthy coping strategies and save the discussion for a later, calmer moment. ... try asking a few questions that empower him to solve the problem: How did it feel when that happened? What did you wish would happen? What can be done differently the next time? ... Young children have a tendency to engage in all-or-nothing thinking. When parents say, “A stop at a theme park might be fun,” young children hear: “We’re going to a park and it will be great!” ... Make a list to indicate hopes, possibilities and sure things. ... Breathe the rainbow — practice deep breathing while thinking about favorite things for each color of the rainbow ... Use art to work through feelings — coloring, drawing and molding clay can all be relaxing
sources.supports: Children can learn to handle disappointment with support; empathic words, time and space to cry and a hug; calm from the parent and the talk later; three questions (how did it feel, what did you wish would happen, what can be done differently next time); young children hear might as will, so a list of hopes, possibilities and sure things; calming skills such as rainbow breathing and drawing. A PBS KIDS for Parents page.

sources.title: How to Help Kids Cope With Disappointment
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents, Katie Hurley, LCSW (16 Jan 2019)
sources.quote: With proper support and frequent discussions about coping with disappointment and overcoming obstacles, young children can learn how to handle life’s disappointments, big and small. ... Use empathic responses like, “I understand that this is difficult. I know you feel disappointed right now.” Give your child the time and space to cry, feel sad and soak up a hug from mom or dad. Connection helps kids recover from adversity. Meet heated responses with calm ones to model healthy coping strategies and save the discussion for a later, calmer moment. ... try asking a few questions that empower him to solve the problem: How did it feel when that happened? What did you wish would happen? What can be done differently the next time? ... Young children have a tendency to engage in all-or-nothing thinking. When parents say, “A stop at a theme park might be fun,” young children hear: “We’re going to a park and it will be great!” ... Make a list to indicate hopes, possibilities and sure things. ... Breathe the rainbow — practice deep breathing while thinking about favorite things for each color of the rainbow ... Use art to work through feelings — coloring, drawing and molding clay can all be relaxing
sources.supports: Children can learn to handle disappointment with support; empathic words, time and space to cry and a hug; calm from the parent and the talk later; three questions (how did it feel, what did you wish would happen, what can be done differently next time); young children hear might as will, so a list of hopes, possibilities and sure things; calming skills such as rainbow breathing and drawing. A PBS KIDS for Parents page.

sources.title: Playful Birthday Party Ideas & Tips for Young Children
sources.publisher: American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org (last updated 31 Aug 2022, adapted from Melissa & Doug)
sources.quote: The rule of thumb for babies and toddlers is your child's age, plus one. So, if your kiddo is turning 3, four attendees is a good number of kid guests. ... Keep the party under 90 minutes for toddlers ... Plan for around 10-15 minutes for each game or activity to keep kids engaged
sources.supports: Guests: the child's age plus one (four for a third birthday); under 90 minutes for toddlers; 10 to 15 minutes per game. An American Academy of Pediatrics family page.

sources.title: Age-by-Age Birthday Party Guide
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents (1 May 2024)
sources.quote: Keep the party to about 90 minutes to avoid over-stimulating them (and exhausting you). ... Five-year-olds know parties are very important and may enjoy the planning even more than the event itself.
sources.supports: A party for three-year-olds of about 90 minutes; five-year-olds may enjoy the planning even more than the party. A PBS KIDS for Parents page.

sources.quote: If appropriate, consider partnering with or even handing off some of the planning responsibilities to your child, or partnering with them for the planning. ... They can pick their favorite theme, games, friends and food.
